notes.meaning: Spring was the normal season when kings led their armies to war, because the heavy winter rains had stopped and food was available in the fields. David sent his general Joab and the army to fight the Ammonites, but David stayed behind in Jerusalem. By staying away from his royal duties on the battlefield, David placed himself in the path of temptation.

David got up from his late-afternoon rest and walked around on the flat roof of his palace to enjoy the cool evening air. From this high viewpoint, he looked down and saw a beautiful woman washing herself in an inner courtyard. Instead of turning away, David lingered and allowed his desires to take control.

David sent someone to find out who the woman was. The servant reported that she was Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite. Both Eliam and Uriah were among David's elite warriors, which should have served as an immediate warning to David to stop.

David sent messengers to bring Bathsheba to the palace, and he slept with her. The text notes that she had just purified herself after her monthly cycle, which proved that any child she conceived would be David's. Afterwards, Bathsheba returned to her own house.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern interpreters view this encounter as an abuse of royal power rather than a consensual affair, since a king held absolute authority and Bathsheba was powerless to refuse.

notes.meaning: Bathsheba discovered that she was pregnant and sent a message to David to let him know. Under God's law given through Moses, adultery was punishable by death for both persons involved. This brief message forced David to face the reality of what he had done.

David sent a message to Joab at the battlefront ordering him to send Uriah back to Jerusalem. Joab obeyed the king's command and sent Uriah. David intended to make it appear that Uriah, not David, was the father of the unborn child.

When Uriah arrived at the palace, David asked him how Joab was doing, how the army was holding up, and how the war was going. These questions were simply an excuse to make the visit seem like an official military report. David hid his real motive behind polite conversation.

David told Uriah to go home and wash his feet, which meant to relax and enjoy the comforts of home. After Uriah left the palace, the king also sent a royal gift of food to his house. David hoped this hospitality would encourage Uriah to sleep with his wife and hide David's sin.

Instead of going home to his wife, Uriah slept at the entrance of the palace among the king's royal guards. As a dedicated soldier, Uriah chose the hardship of military duty over personal comfort. In God's providence, Uriah's loyalty began to unravel David's secret plan.

The servants told David the next morning that Uriah had not gone down to his house. David summoned Uriah and asked why he had refused to go home after such a long journey. David continued to act like a caring leader while secretly plotting to protect himself.

Uriah answered that the ark of God, the soldiers of Israel, and his commander Joab were all living in tents out in the open battlefield. He swore an oath that he could not bring himself to eat, drink, and sleep with his wife while his fellow soldiers faced danger. Uriah's honor and godliness stood in sharp contrast to David's selfish deceit.

David told Uriah to remain in Jerusalem for another day and promised to send him back to the army tomorrow. Uriah stayed at the court for that day and the next. David bought himself more time to come up with another scheme.

David invited Uriah to eat and drink with him at the royal table and got him drunk. Even with his senses dulled by wine, Uriah went back out in the evening to sleep on his mat with the palace guards rather than going home. Uriah's deep sense of duty remained firm despite David's dishonest tricks.

The next morning, David wrote a secret letter to Joab and sent it directly in Uriah's hands. David used Uriah's complete honesty against him, knowing he would deliver the sealed message without reading it. The innocent soldier carried his own death sentence back to the camp.

In the letter, David commanded Joab to place Uriah at the very front where the fighting was most dangerous, and then pull the troops back from him so he would be killed. Because his attempts to hide his adultery had failed, David turned to cold-blooded murder. Sin rapidly deepens when a person refuses to confess it.

While carrying out the siege against Rabbah, Joab positioned Uriah at a section of the city wall where he knew the strongest enemy fighters were stationed. Joab obeyed the king's wicked order without question. He showed that he cared more about staying in royal favor than protecting an innocent man.

The defenders of the city charged out from the gates and fought against Joab's men. During the clash, several Israelite soldiers were killed, and Uriah the Hittite died with them. David's plot succeeded, but it also cost the lives of other faithful soldiers.

After the battle, Joab sent a messenger to Jerusalem to deliver a full report of what had happened. He wanted the king to hear how the siege was progressing. This official report was also designed to deliver the news David was waiting for.

Joab gave specific instructions to the messenger on how to deliver the report. He told him to tell the whole story of the battle first before saying anything else. Joab carefully planned how to manage the king's reaction.

Joab warned the messenger that the king might become angry about the tactical mistake of leading troops too close to the city wall, where archers could easily shoot them down. Military leaders knew that charging near a fortified wall was dangerous. Joab anticipated David's questions so the messenger would be prepared.

Joab reminded the messenger of Israel's history, when Abimelech was killed at Thebez because a woman dropped a millstone on him from a wall. If David asked why the army had made the same foolish mistake, the messenger was instructed to say that Uriah the Hittite was dead too. Joab knew that news of Uriah's death would instantly quiet David's anger.

The messenger traveled to Jerusalem and reported everything Joab had ordered him to say. He stood before David to deliver the update from the battlefield. The message carried both the news of a military loss and the outcome of David's secret order.

The messenger explained that the Ammonites came out of the city and pushed the Israelite troops back into the open field, but Israel rallied and drove them back to the entrance of the city gate. This part of the account showed that the troops fought bravely. It also explained why the men ended up so close to the dangerous walls.

The messenger reported that archers shot arrows down from the wall, killing several of the king's soldiers, and he concluded by stating that Uriah the Hittite was dead as well. Instead of waiting for David to get angry, the messenger delivered the news of Uriah right away. The message informed David that his deadly plot was complete.

David told the messenger to comfort Joab and say that the sword kills one soldier just like another in war. He instructed Joab to press the attack and tear down the city. David showed a chilling lack of grief over Uriah and the other fallen men, brushing aside their deaths as ordinary bad luck.

When Bathsheba learned that her husband Uriah was dead, she observed the customary period of mourning for him. In Israelite tradition, this mourning usually lasted seven days. It gave a public appearance of grief while preparing the way for what would happen next.

As soon as the mourning ended, David brought Bathsheba into his palace, married her, and she gave birth to a son. To the public, it appeared that David was simply showing kindness to the widow of a fallen hero. The final line delivers God's verdict: the thing David had done was evil in the eyes of the Lord.
